lessons.title: Ethos, pathos, logos
lessons.tip: Aristotle named three ways to persuade: ethos (trust: who is speaking), pathos (feeling: stories and emotions) and logos (logic: facts and reasons). Strong persuasion often uses all three.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): ethos, pathos, logos
Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes, and Cialdini’s influence principles (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Know your audience
lessons.tip: Persuasion works best when you know your audience: what they care about, what they already know and what they worry about. Use their words, give benefits that matter to them, and answer their worries before they ask.

lessons.title: Persuade or manipulate?
lessons.tip: Ethical persuasion is honest: true facts, real benefits and respect for the other person’s choice. Manipulation uses lies, pressure, fear or tricks to stop people from thinking. Ask: would I be happy if they knew exactly what I was doing?
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): ethos, pathos, logos
Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes, and Cialdini’s influence principles (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Interests, not positions
lessons.tip: A position is what someone says they want: “I want the window open.” An interest is why: “I need fresh air.” Two people can have opposite positions and still share interests. Ask “why?” to find the interest, then look for a deal that meets both.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): ethos, pathos, logos
Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes, and Cialdini’s influence principles (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Say no politely
lessons.tip: You can refuse and still keep a good relationship. Thank the person, say no clearly, give a short reason if you wish, and offer another choice. Softening words such as “unfortunately” and “I’m afraid” make the no gentler. Do not say “maybe” if you mean no.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): ethos, pathos, logos
Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes, and Cialdini’s influence principles (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Prepare before you talk
lessons.tip: Strong negotiators prepare three numbers or points. Your target is what you hope to get. Your limit is the worst result you will accept. Your best alternative is what you will do if there is no deal. Knowing your best alternative keeps you calm, because you can say no. Think about the other side too: what do they need most?
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): ethos, pathos and logos
Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes (1981), as a source of ideas: interests, options and a best alternative (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Make the first offer
lessons.tip: The first number often sets the range for the talk. If you know the market, start with a bold but reasonable offer and give a reason: “I would like 220 dollars, because the bike has new tires.” A reason makes a number feel fair. Avoid a number you cannot defend. When the other side starts, do not jump to the middle at once; ask about their reasons first.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): ethos, pathos and logos
Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes (1981), as a source of ideas: interests, options and a best alternative (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Trade, don’t give in
lessons.tip: Giving in means you lose something and get nothing. Trading means you give something and ask for something. Use “if… then…”: “If you can pay today, I can lower the price.” Look for things that cost you little but matter to them, such as speed, a warranty, or a clear schedule. Trade one point at a time and keep a list of what you have given.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): ethos, pathos and logos
Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes (1981), as a source of ideas: interests, options and a best alternative (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Ask and listen
lessons.tip: Good negotiators learn before they push. Ask open questions: “What matters most to you in this deal?” Then stay quiet and listen. Show you heard by naming the feeling or the need: “It sounds like speed is the most important point for you.” People often say the real reason after a short silence. Take notes and repeat key words back.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): ethos, pathos and logos
Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes (1981), as a source of ideas: interests, options and a best alternative (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Handle objections
lessons.tip: An objection is a reason someone says no. Do not argue at once. First, acknowledge it: “I understand the price is a worry.” Second, ask a question to understand it: “Compared with what?” Third, answer with a fact or an option. Often the objection is not the real problem, so listen for what sits behind it.

lessons.title: Firm and friendly
lessons.tip: You can say no and stay friendly. Give a reason, then offer what you can do: “I can’t move the deadline, but I can send a draft on Wednesday.” Say the same message calmly if the person pushes again; this is called the broken record. lessons.title: Interests, options and criteria
lessons.tip: Move the talk from positions to interests and then to options. Ask what each side needs and why. Brainstorm several options before you judge them. lessons.title: Strengthen your alternative
lessons.tip: Your power comes less from toughness than from your best alternative. Before a talk, improve it: ask a second supplier for a quote, check another job offer, prepare a fallback plan. Estimate the other side’s alternative too; if theirs is weak, you may ask for more. Never bluff about an alternative you do not have. If you are asked, say what is true: “I have options, and I would prefer to work with you.”

Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes (1981), and later negotiation research (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Packages and trade-offs
lessons.tip: When there are several issues, negotiate them together as a package rather than one by one. Each side values the issues differently, so you can trade what costs you little for what matters to them: this is how both gain. Offer two or three equivalent packages and see which one they prefer: it reveals their priorities. Avoid agreeing to a single issue early, because you lose your flexibility.

lessons.title: Respond to an extreme first offer
lessons.tip: If the other side opens with an extreme number, do not let it set the range. Do not counter at once with a number that moves toward theirs. Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes (1981), and later negotiation research (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Across cultures
lessons.tip: Communication styles differ across cultures and organizations. In some contexts people say “no” directly; in others they say “this will be difficult” and expect you to understand. Silence can mean thinking, respect or disagreement. Some groups decide in the meeting; others decide afterward with seniors. Do not assume your own style is the standard. Ask politely how decisions are made, and check meaning: “Do I understand that this is not possible?”

Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes (1981), and later negotiation research (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.tip: Some negotiators use pressure: false deadlines, a good cop and a bad cop, a final offer that is not final, or asking for a small extra at the end (“nibbling”). lessons.title: Authority and approval
lessons.tip: Many deals need approval from someone not in the room. Find out early who decides and what they care about: “Who else will weigh in on this?” If the other person says “I must check with my director,” ask how you can help her present the case: “Would a one-page summary help?” Make sure you have authority too: say what you can commit to today and what needs approval. Avoid agreeing in principle when the real decision sits elsewhere.

Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes (1981), and later negotiation research (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Repair and renegotiate
lessons.tip: Deals sometimes go wrong. If you must renegotiate or repair trust, begin with facts and responsibility, not blame: “We missed the delivery date. Here is what happened and what we propose.” Acknowledge the impact on the other side, offer a concrete fix, and ask what they need. When you renegotiate a signed deal, explain what changed and keep the parts that still work. The aim is a working relationship, not a win.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): ethos, pathos and logos
Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes (1981), and later negotiation research (concepts only; no text copied)
